outcomes: Map matrix notation to row-major offsets for nonsquare shapes
Explain how loop order changes spatial locality
Implement a cache-blocked scalar matrix multiplication with edge tiles
Reuse and correctly clear output storage
Benchmark multiple correct kernels without claiming a predetermined winner

row-major.name: Row-major order
row-major.definition: A contiguous layout in which all columns of a row are stored before the next row.
row-major.explanation: For a matrix with n columns, coordinate (i,j) maps to i×n+j. Changing j by one accesses adjacent values, while changing i by one jumps a complete row. The layout does not change matrix algebra, but it changes which loop orders use cache lines effectively. This chapter stores A, B, and C in row-major vectors and uses nonsquare shapes so an accidental transpose cannot hide behind equal dimensions.

cache-locality.name: Cache locality
cache-locality.definition: Access patterns that reuse recently fetched data or nearby addresses.
cache-locality.explanation: Temporal locality reuses the same value before it leaves a fast memory level. Spatial locality uses neighboring values brought in by the same cache line. In row-major matrix multiplication, an inner j loop walks adjacent B and C entries while reusing one A scalar. Locality often reduces expensive data movement, but the performance effect depends on shape, cache hierarchy, compiler, and competing work, so it remains a measurement question.

cache-blocking.name: Cache blocking
cache-blocking.definition: Partitioning loops into smaller tiles so a working set can be reused in cache.
cache-blocking.explanation: A blocked matrix multiplication steps through subranges of rows, shared indices, and columns before moving to another tile. Edge tiles use shorter ranges when dimensions are not divisible by the block size. The mathematical products are unchanged, though their accumulation grouping may differ. Block size is hardware- and shape-dependent: a small tile adds overhead, while a large tile may exceed cache. The reference keeps one explicit value for learners to measure and tune.

allocation-reuse.name: Allocation reuse
allocation-reuse.definition: Keeping an owned buffer across repeated operations and overwriting it for each result.
allocation-reuse.explanation: Training and inference often repeat operations with stable shapes. Allocating a new output inside each kernel call mixes allocator cost with arithmetic and increases latency variation. Passing a mutable slice lets the caller allocate once. Accumulating kernels must still clear the slice exactly once before adding contributions; reuse never permits stale values. End-to-end measurements may include allocation when the application really performs it, but kernel comparisons should use identical preallocated storage.
